 WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (CBS12) — Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks is encouraging property owners to document and report significant flood damage to her office.
 Palm Beach County homeowners whose homes were damaged by recent flooding may qualify for a partial property tax refund if the damage left their residence uninhabitable for at least 30 consecutive days, the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser’s Office said Tuesday.
 Homeowners seeking a refund must file an Application for Catastrophic Event Tax Refund, Form DR-465 , with the Property Appraiser’s Office by March 1, 2027, and provide supporting documents. The office recommends keeping photos and videos of damage, insurance information, utility bills, contractor statements and building permits.
 Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks urged owners to report significant damage as soon as possible. Residents displaced by flooding should update their mailing addresses with both the Property Appraiser’s Office and the Palm Beach County Tax Collector so they receive notices.
 The county says flood damage will not change a property’s 2026 assessment because Florida properties are assessed based on their condition on Jan. 1 each year. Damage that remains unrepaired on Jan. 1, 2027, may affect the 2027 assessment. Homeowners may also be able to keep their homestead exemption and Save Our Homes assessment benefits while rebuilding if they meet applicable requirements.
 See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes 
 Property taxes remain due even if a home is damaged or destroyed. To qualify for the refund, homeowners must pay their 2026 property taxes by March 31, 2027, the county said.
 Commercial and other non-residential properties do not qualify for the catastrophic event refund. However, damage still present on Jan. 1, 2027, will be reflected in the 2027 assessment, and rebuilt improvements may retain the 10% assessment limitation.
 Neighboring counties
 The other four counties have existing property-damage guidance and form:
 Martin County: The Property Appraiser’s website advises owners to report damage as soon as possible. It outlines the 30-day uninhabitable threshold for a potential residential tax refund, the March 1 filing deadline and how damage and repairs may affect a later assessment. 
 St. Lucie County: The Property Appraiser’s website provides the DR-465 application and a catastrophic event property damage guide. 
 Indian River County: The Property Appraiser lists the DR-465 application among its available forms.
 Okeechobee County: The Property Appraiser has a property damage reporting form that asks whether a home was uninhabitable, destroyed or left its occupants displaced for 30 days or more. Its DR-465 form page says applications are due by March 1 of the year after the event.
 The Palm Beach County Property Appraiser’s Office says owners with substantial structural damage can call 561-355-2866 . More information and the county’s damage-reporting instructions are available at pbcpao.gov/storm-damaged.htm .
